newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - France's top insurer is no fan of long hours.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - France's top insurer is no fan of long hours.

text.p: Claude Bebear, who transformed Axa from a regional French insurer into the world's second largest in just two decades, does not believe in working too hard.

"There are so many other things to discover in life," says the 62-year-old Axa chairman who practises what he preaches, spending four days a week at the office. Besides, "if you work too much, you get tired and aren't clear-headed."

Bebear, a big game hunter whose office walls are studded with trophies, has needed a clear head to forge an acquisition strategy that has turned Axa into a sprawling realm with activities in 50 countries and five continents.

His latest coup, however, was at home with the 40 billion franc ($6.7 billion) takeover, completed in May, of France's largest insurer, UAP. The operation, which he billed as the "deal of the century," vaulted Axa into second place in the world insurance premium income league, just behind Japan's Nippon Life.
Bebear, a genial man with a spring in his step, had wanted to be a surgeon but his schoolteacher father said he would be better off in engineering because of his ability with figures.
GRADUATED NEAR BOTTOM OF THE CLASS

He won entry into the prestigious Ecole Polytechnique but missed lessons because of his work as class treasurer and graduated 204th. When he was ready to find a job, there were no big name employers knocking at his door.

He wound up being recruited in 1958 by a Normandy mutual company, Anciennes Mutuelles, where he learned the ropes of the insurance trade. "I got into insurance by chance," he said in an interview with Reuters.

Anciennes Mutuelles -- renamed Axa in 1985 because it could be easily pronounced in all languages -- was the 24th largest insurance firm in France. How small it was can be gauged by the fact that in those days there were no big French insurers.

"When I entered the field, insurance was a bit secondary," he recalls. "The big insurance companies in France were all medium-sized businesses. Insurance didn't have the importance it has in today's society."
But the job had its advantages. "I liked the man who hired me," he says. "Because it was a small company, I was the heir apparent. I was in management right away and I enjoyed that.
A spell in Canada to set up a subsidiary taught him the company would have to spread its wings to flourish.
"I thought France was the salt of the earth. Over there, I learned...the company would have to be international to spread its risks and always be present on a buoyant market," he says.
MODUS OPERANDI -- BUYING UP DISTRESSED COMPANIES
Global diversification became one of his watchwords -- and now just 20 percent of Axa's profits come from France.

By 1975 he was chairman of the company. Seven years later, Bebear made his first major acquisition, swallowing up the Drouot insurance group, and he established his modus operandi -- buying distressed companies and turning them around.
"Drouot was twice our size and, on top of that, it was losing twice what we were earning," he said.
"Everyone said we would fall flat on our face. But we knew the company well. We knew its fundamentals were good and its problems were just due to management errors," he says.
"When everyone thinks something is bad and you know it's good, that's when you have opportunities," he adds. At the start, without a big war chest, Axa had to look for bargains.
Other takeovers followed. In 1986 Axa became France's second largest insurer, behind UAP, after the purchase of Presence.

In 1991, Bebear achieved his goal of establishing a big presence in the United States, buying Equitable Cos, an insurance, fund management and merchant bank conglomerate, which had been written off by financial markets but has turned into a money-spinner for Axa.
"We were sure it was a very good company that was on the road to recovery," he says. "But our share price dropped by half. It recovered and everyone now says we did a good deal."
INSURANCE AND ASSET MANAGEMENT THE FOCUS
Another of his rules has been that the target "has to be in line with what we do -- insurance and asset management."
This singlemindness saved Axa's profits from being slashed in France's 1990s real estate slump. It alone of the big insurers and banks did not have any huge writeoffs when prices collapsed.
In fact, when property values began soaring in the 1980s, Axa started selling its real estate -- getting top prices.
"When I saw the really sharp rise in real estate prices, I had an instinctive peasant's reflex which said: 'This can't last like that, so it's probably time to sell,' " saids Bebear.

Similarly, he was not seduced by property development, the great vogue of the 1980s, "because it was a question of focus. We would be getting out of our core business and I knew it could be dangerous and you could lose a lot of money."
Axa's only departure from insurance has been into Bebear's hobby, which is wines.

It has a special wine subsidiary, which owns chateaux in Burgundy and Bordeaux. But even in these investments, Axa has tried to find bargains, seeking out rundown estates in hopes they can be turned round.
SPRINGBOARD FOR ASIA

After Equitable, Axa went after Australian life insurer National Mutual in 1995, to use it as a springboard for the Asia-Pacific region, which Bebear believes will be the great growth market for insurance in the next century.
National Mutual was forced to seek a white knight, partly because of over-rapid expansion, but now is back on track.
Axa recently achieved a long-held ambition when it won permission from Beijing authorities to sell insurance in China.
In 1996, Axa surprised markets by going after former state owned UAP, worried it would be taken over by a foreign insurer. The deal created a group with turnover of 320 billion francs.

It raised eyebrows among some analysts who feared Axa's go-getting style and profit-minded culture might be diluted by association with UAP's corporate culture, generally viewed as stodgy and bureaucratic.

But others said the two firms were well matched, with Axa strong in the United States and Asia and UAP owning Colonia, Germany's second largest non-life insurer, as well as big operations in Belgium and Britain. Only in France is there a major overlap between the two partners.
Bebear is aware it is one thing to buy a company and another to make a success of the purchase. Axa makes a big effort not to treat subsidiaries as "colonies".
"When we buy a company, those people are members of the same team and we forget where they come from. Everyone is a member of the same family."
THINK GLOBAL, ACT LOCAL
Axa operates with local management. Bebear likes to quote the maxim: "Think global, act local,"
"Management must be able to decide quickly and it must be people from the country because they're more accepted and they know the market better than someone from the outside," he said.

Having finally made the world Axa's oyster, the company will spend a couple of years digesting UAP. But Bebear says there will be more acquisitions ahead in the face of the wave of consolidation sweeping the insurance sector.
The big challenge for Axa now is to boost its profitability to levels of international rivals. Axa is aiming for 15 percent return on equity, up from 10.2 percent in 1996.

Bebear has said he wants to retire in three years at 65. So far there are no clear-cut contenders mentioned to succeed him. But insiders say his team-work approach means there will be no shortage of qualified individuals within Axa to replace him.
($ = 5.936 FRENCH FRANCS)
